In the [[theory of computation]], the '''Sudan function''' is an example of a [[function (mathematics)|function]] that is [[recursion#Functional recursion|recursive]], but not [[primitive recursive function|primitive recursive]]. This is also true of the better-known [[Ackermann function]].

In 1926, [[David Hilbert]] conjectured that every computable function was primitive recursive. This was refuted by [[Gabriel Sudan]] and [[Wilhelm Ackermann]] {{mdash}} both his students {{mdash}} using different functions that were published in quick succession: Sudan in 1927,{{sfn|Sudan|1927}} Ackermann in 1928.{{sfn|Ackermann|1928}}

The Sudan function is the earliest published example of a recursive function that is not primitive recursive.{{sfn|Calude|Marcus|Tevy|1979}}

==Definition==

<math display="block">\begin{array}{lll}
F_0 (x, y) & = x+y \\
F_{n+1} (x, 0) & = x & \text{if } n \ge 0 \\
F_{n+1} (x, y+1) & = F_n (F_{n+1} (x, y), F_{n+1} (x, y) + y + 1) & \text{if } n\ge 0 \\
\end{array}</math>
The last equation can be equivalently written as
<math display="block">\begin{array}{lll}
F_{n+1} (x, y+1) & = F_n(F_{n+1} (x, y), F_0(F_{n+1}(x, y), y + 1)) \\
\end{array}</math>.{{sfn|Calude|1988|page=92}}

==Computation==
These equations can be used as rules of a [[Rewriting#Term rewriting systems|term rewriting system (TRS)]].

The generalized function <math>F(x,y,n) \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} F_n(x,y)</math> leads to the rewrite rules
:<math>\begin{array}{lll}
\text{(r1)} & F(x, y, 0) & \rightarrow x+y \\
\text{(r2)} & F(x, 0, n+1) & \rightarrow x \\
\text{(r3)} & F(x, y+1, n+1) & \rightarrow F(F(x, y, n+1), F(F(x, y, n+1), y + 1,0), n) \\
\end{array}</math>

At each reduction step the rightmost innermost occurrence of F is rewritten, by application of one of the rules (r1) - (r3).

Calude (1988) gives an '''example''': compute <math>F(2,2,1) \rightarrow_{*} 12</math>.{{sfn|Calude|1988|pages=92-95}}

The reduction sequence is<ref>The rightmost innermost occurrences of F are underlined.</ref>
:{|
|-
|<math>\underline{{F(2,2,1)}}</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r3} F(F(2,1,1),F(\underline{{F(2,1,1)}},2,0),0)</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r3} F(F(2,1,1),F(F(F(2,0,1),F(\underline{{F(2,0,1)}},1,0),0),2,0),0)</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r2} F(F(2,1,1),F(F(F(2,0,1),\underline{{F(2,1,0)}},0),2,0),0)</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r1} F(F(2,1,1),F(F(\underline{{F(2,0,1)}},3,0),2,0),0)</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r2} F(F(2,1,1),F(\underline{{F(2,3,0)}},2,0),0)</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r1} F(F(2,1,1),\underline{{F(5,2,0)}},0)</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r1} F(\underline{{F(2,1,1)}},7,0)</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r3} F(F(F(2,0,1),F(\underline{{F(2,0,1)}},1,0),0),7,0)</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r2} F(F(F(2,0,1),\underline{{F(2,1,0)}},0),7,0)</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r1} F(F(\underline{{F(2,0,1)}},3,0),7,0)</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r2} F(\underline{{F(2,3,0)}},7,0)</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r1} \underline{{F(5,7,0)}}</math>
|-
|{{space|4}}<math>\rightarrow_{r1} 12</math>
|}
